content.text:
**Bun 1.4** is the latest major release (August 20, 2026) of Bun, a fast all-in-one JavaScript and TypeScript runtime, package manager, test runner, and bundler designed as a drop-in replacement for Node.js.[[1]](https://bun.com/blog/bun-v1.4)

### Key Highlights
- **Rewritten in Rust**: This is the first version fully rewritten from Zig to Rust (Bun 1.3.14 was the last Zig version). The JavaScript engine remains JavaScriptCore (from WebKit), so JS/TS behavior is unchanged, but the surrounding runtime, HTTP server, bundler, and package manager are now in Rust. This improves memory safety, reduces binary size (~20% smaller), and enables better compile-time checks.[[2]](https://gihyo.jp/article/2026/08/bun-1.4)
- **Node.js Compatibility**: Passes **+1,517** more tests from the Node.js test suite—the largest jump since Bun 1.0. Many core modules (`node:http`, `node:fs`, `node:cluster`, etc.) now pass 97–100% of Node’s own tests. This enables better support for frameworks like Next.js 16, Playwright, Vitest, and OpenTelemetry. It also reports as Node.js 26.[[3]](https://appwrite.io/blog/post/announcing-bun-1-4-runtime)
- **Performance Gains**:
  - Idle CPU usage reduced by up to **5x**.
  - Memory usage cut by up to **35–48%** (especially for HTTP servers; e.g., Express memory dropped from 169 MB to 92 MB in some benchmarks).
  - Startup **50% faster** on Linux (hello-world in ~5.1 ms vs. 10.9 ms in 1.3; Node 26 is ~27 ms) and **2.5x faster** on Windows.
  - Many operations are significantly faster (e.g., Markdown parsing 138×, certain Buffer decoding 8–46×, Promises 1.5–2.4×, source map decoding 3.1×).[[1]](https://bun.com/blog/bun-v1.4)

### New Built-in APIs (Reducing Dependencies)
Bun 1.4 adds several high-performance native APIs to replace common npm packages and shrink your dependency tree:[[4]](https://www.stork.ai/blog/bun-14-the-update-that-kills-your-dependencies)

- **`Bun.Image`** — Fast image processing (replaces Sharp).
- **`Bun.WebView`** — Headless browser automation (replaces Puppeteer/Playwright). Uses system WebKit on macOS or drives Chrome/Edge via CDP on other platforms. Supports navigation, clicking, JS evaluation, screenshots, etc.
- **`Bun.markdown`** — Native Markdown rendering (replaces Marked; up to 138× faster).
- **`Bun.cron()`** — Built-in cron job scheduler (replaces node-cron).
- **`Bun.Terminal`** — PTY (pseudo-terminal) support (replaces node-pty).
- Native `JSON5` parser (`Bun.JSON5.parse/stringify`).
- Native streams (`ReadableStream`, `WritableStream`, `TransformStream`, `CompressionStream`, etc.).
- Faster `bun:ffi` (up to ~3–3.8×).
- Experimental HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 support in `Bun.serve()` and `fetch()`.
- Other CLI improvements: `bun run --parallel`, `bun test --parallel`, `bun audit fix`, `bun dedupe`, `bun prune`, improved `bun repl`, Markdown pretty-printing with `bun ./README.md`, directory serving, Range/conditional requests, and Windows ARM64 support.

The bundler now supports compiling entire frontends (including React, JSX, TypeScript, CSS, images) into a **single self-contained HTML file** with `--compile --target=browser`. The React compiler is now built into `bun build` and is over 19× faster than via Babel.[[5]](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i38DgEuaJwM)

### Production & Memory Improvements
Bun 1.4 unifies memory allocation under mimalloc (replacing the dual JavaScriptCore + mimalloc setup). It adds a scavenger thread, partial page clearing, and better lazy zeroing, leading to lower idle CPU and faster memory reclamation in long-running apps.[[1]](https://bun.com/blog/bun-v1.4)

### How to Install or Upgrade
```bash
bun upgrade
```
Or fresh install:
```bash
curl -fsSL https://bun.sh/install | bash
```

Official release notes: [https://bun.com/blog/bun-v1.4](https://bun.com/blog/bun-v1.4)[[1]](https://bun.com/blog/bun-v1.4)

Bun continues to focus on speed, reducing external dependencies, and improving Node compatibility while providing a more complete standard library for JavaScript/TypeScript development. Some community discussion around the Rust rewrite has been mixed, but benchmarks show clear wins in performance and compatibility.
